item.description: The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. That season, Tarik Skubal, Paul Skenes, Garrett Crochet and Zack Wheeler were the top four pitchers drafted. Per our Fantasy Player Rater, Skubal ($35.5), Crochet ($32.8) and Skenes ($30.8) finished 1-2-3 among starting pitchers in all roto formats. Wheeler finished 14th ($22.6) despite his season being cut short. As is the case every single year, to varying degrees, there were mid-round arms who produced elite roto seasons (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Max Fried), as well starters such as Nathan Eovaldi, Matthew Boyd, and Trevor Rogers who provided hefty profit a as late-round picks and free agent acquisitions.
As is also the case every season, there were early-round landmines. Cole Ragans, Blake Snell, and Corbin Burnes all missed at least two-thirds of the season due to injuries. Logan Gilbert investors certainly weren’t thrilled about his abbreviated season with only six wins. Nevertheless, dream seasons from the Crème de la crème instilled an illusion of tranquility at the top of the SP pool for 2026 drafts despite the position’s inherent risks and volatile history.
The calm ominously turned to storm on Opening Day. Paul Skenes couldn’t get out of the first inning against the Mets, allowing five earned runs, as droves of social media melodramatics scolded us: “…and that’s why you never draft pitchers early!” Skenes (174 IP – 200 K – 10 W – 3.82 – 1.12) inevitably lost “fantasy god” status as his price dropped a couple of rounds for 2027 drafts. Skubal was a top 10 pitcher with elite ratios, but did not have his usual season of dominance due to missing 5-6 starts. Crochet was an injury landmine and one of many early-round busts.
There were some wins in the second tier (Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale) as well as disappointments (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Ragans again), but what may be most memorable about last season’s starting pitcher pool was that leagues were won without having to invest in early starting pitchers at all. Of course, that only happened to managers who side-stepped the early-round hitter landmines like Aaron Judge, Ronald Acuña Jr., Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Francisco Lindor and Cal Raleigh. The two top producers – Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler – were post-100 ADP picks. Of the 19 starters who earned $14 or more in 12-team leagues, 13 had an ADP of 100+, including six with an ADP of 250 or greater.

Wheeler recovered thoroughly from his thoracic outlet procedure and produced yet another $20+ season: 162 IP (28 starts) – 193 K – 14 W – 3.00 – 1.05. He has been the best pitcher in the Majors since 2021, leading in wins (79), ERA (2.92) and second in strikeouts (1,234) behind Cease’s 1,345.
Chase Burns will be highly coveted after his masterful performance over his first full season (154.1 IP – 185 K – 15 W – 2.86 – 1.17) and will be drafted among the top 12 to 15 starters. Nolan McLean will be slightly cheaper than Burns after his first full and successful season in the Majors. Cases made against either this offseason will start with concerns about their lack of elite control and potential WHIP damage at Tier 2 SP prices. Eury Pérez is in this boat as well after posting a 10.3% walk rate and a 1.21 WHIP, though don’t expect to pay anything but a premium for the coveted fireballer who will turn 24 in April.
Joe Ryan should be a solid pick among the top 100 as well. Though he may never have that 180+ IP dream season where good health and all the cards align, Ryan has been a dependable fantasy stud, posting a K-BB% over 20% for four straight seasons and has made between 23 and 30 starts over his first five full seasons.
There were quite a few negative value guys in this range, which was quite shocking for some: George Kirby, Kyle Bradish, Framber Valdez, Kevin Gausman and Emmet Sheehan. Kirby is quickly becoming persona non grata in the fantasy community, posting a painful 1.40 WHIP last season and two straight years with a 4.00+ ERA. Bradish’s WHIP (1.42) was even worse than Kirby’s as he did most of his damage after the All-Star break, posting a 5.29 ERA and a .398 wOBA in those final 10 starts before getting shelved due to lower abdominal pain and being diagnosed with a sports hernia. Gausman compiled 30+ starts for a sixth consecutive season. A long list of names, so we’ll just touch on a few of them. Among the studs who provided tremendous profit were Cade Cavalli, Reid Detmers, Nick Martinez, Payton Tolle, and the impenetrable Eduardo Rodriguez, who pulled off 17 wins with a 2.89 ERA despite a much higher xFIP (4.44) and SIERA (4.62) and the lowest BABIP (.274 of his career). I don’t usually mess with the peripheral gods and will stubbornly skip over him in early drafts. Cade Cavalli had an epic run after the All-Star break, posting a 90:16 K:BB and a 1.90 ERA over his final 12 starts. Reid Detmers was having a decent season, but really began to shine when the Angels fired pitching coach Mike Maddux. Over those final 8 starts, Detmers posted a 4-0 record with a 1.62 ERA and an impressive 55:5 K:BB. Angels fans are hoping that the new regime under new owner Stan Kroenke will bring the organization from the basement to at least the living room. Interim GM John Mozeliak will stay in the role for now and help the Angels find a permanent GM and a new manager, since Kurt Suzuki is one-and-done.
A $1.20 earning shouldn’t detract from the admiration that Clay Holmes should receive after Round 15 in 12-teamers. He produced a respectable 3.29 ERA, but his low value was impacted by a low strikeout rate (18.6%), six wins, and time spent on the IL, which led to just 18 starts on the season. Michael Wacha was stellar yet again, earning $10 in 12-team NFBC roto leagues as the SP29. Taj Bradley, Troy Melton, Ian Seymour, Justin Wrobleski, and Michael Soroka all had some strong stretches of production that helped fantasy managers, especially those who got out of the Wrobleski business before that ship began to sank. Seymour and Melton are already earning some early 2027 draft love, getting scooped up among the top 50 starters in the 150-175 ADP range — a price that is likely to surge as we move through the heart of draft season.
Finally, a shout out to FAAB stud Sean Burke who broke out in a big way. He produced a 3.34 ERA, a 1.20 WHIP and punched out 185 batters over 172.1 innings. Burke had a scorching-hot nine-start run from June 18 through August 11 where he rocked a 1.60 ERA and struck out 79, with just 11 walks over 62 innings. He had some rough starts, but was still worth every free agent penny. Based on some of the prices (2-5% of budget), it almost felt like pennies were what were being spent.
It’s always a good idea to dig into player stats not long after the season has ended. It helps avoid building biases that may fester, resonate, and solidify within our draft tendencies for the coming draft season. When we wait too long into the winter to review individual player profiles, we increase the likelihood of outside influences manipulating our valuations of players — whether it’s articles that do a good job of convincing a player is a boon or a bust, social media bandwaggoning, or ADP data itself. We don’t have to decide between Ashcraft and McLean now, but if we’re equipped with the details of their stats, underlying metrics, velocity trends, pitch mix changes, Stuff, and healthy history, we can limit emotion and bias from our decision-making and make optimal, objective decisions during the heart of draft season.

The World Series is about to begin, and we’re being treated to a doozy of a series between the Brewers and the Rays. However, for the 28 other teams, they are turning their attention to 2027, so we’ll join them in that for a bit with some starting pitcher rankings for next season.
This is now my fourth year publishing my starting pitcher rankings and my second year doing it this early. In many ways, I like doing a first pass at rankings this year. At this point, it’s hard to overthink. Most players aren’t playing games or posting videos of new pitches, so there is nothing to get geeked about. Instead, these rankings are more “gut feel” rankings based on how I feel about all of these pitchers at the end of the season. While I tried not to get too in the weeds about stats, I did look back at the general profile that allowed a pitcher to finish among the top 30 overall starters in recent years, and tried to prioritize pitchers who fit that profile, which mostly meant elevating pitchers who get swings and misses, and penalizing pitchers who don’t seem like a good bet for a full season of innings.
As always, the pitchers are split into tiers based on their skillset or what they’ll provide your fantasy team. The tiers themselves are more important than the rankings inside the tiers, so I wouldn’t split hairs over a few spots in the rankings. I’ve also ranked these pitchers as if I’m doing a 12-team league, so safe but boring low-end starters take a hit in value, etc. I won’t have really long write-ups here, but I’ll be back with updated rankings after the new year, where we can get a little more into the nitty-gritty of the rankings.

item.content:encoded:
Assuming something resembling a normal MLB offseason emerges from the rubble of CBA negotiations this winter, two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal could be in line for a record-setting payday for a pitcher.
At the very least, he's a lock to exceed $200 million in his first trip to free agency. He could be eyeing a $400 million mega deal as one of the best pitchers to ever hit the open market.
There is a steep drop-off in earning power behind him in this year's free-agent class, but there are high-profile extension candidates across baseball, and more and more teams are making an early push to lock up young talent.
Ahead, we've taken a shot at predicting the next 10 players who will sign $200 million contracts, with age, production, long-term outlook and proximity to free agency all factors in building the list.
2B/SS CJ Abrams
1 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2028
Whether he is the centerpiece of a blockbuster deal or a foundational building block for the Nationals, CJ Abrams has put himself in position for a massive payday following a career year offensively.
Still only 26 years old, he posted a 127 OPS+ with 30 doubles, 33 home runs, 106 RBI and 34 steals in a 5.1-WAR season, earning his second All-Star selection in the last three years.
Despite his defensive shortcomings and a potential long-term move to second base, his age and offensive impact make him an obvious candidate for a lucrative extension and the potential headliner of the 2028-29 free-agent class.
Even as a second baseman, he will have a strong case to eclipse the seven-year, $175 million deal that Marcus Semien signed with the Rangers prior to his age-31 season.
DH Yordan Alvarez
2 of 10
Contract Status: Two years, $53.7 million remaining on contract
Teams buying out the final year or two of a superstar's contract to lock him up with a fresh long-term extension is common practice. No one is a more obvious candidate for that approach than presumptive AL MVP Yordan Alvarez.
With two years remaining on his six-year, $115 million extension, and fresh off a season where he hit .316/.432/.601 with 42 home runs and 106 RBI to make a run at AL Triple Crown honors, he is unquestionably one of the game's elite offensive talents.
His back-loaded current deal will pay him $26.8 million in 2027 and 2028, so replacing those two years with a fresh long-term deal and an AAV somewhere in the $30 million range would not actually be tacking that much onto the payroll next year.
The Astros could also decide it's time to rebuild, which would make him a blockbuster trade chip and an obvious extension candidate for any team that ponies up the prospect talent to land him.
3B Junior Caminero
3 of 10
Contract Status: Pre-arbitration, controllable through 2030
Junior Caminero will not reach arbitration for the first time until after the 2027 season. At that point, he might be in line for a record-setting payday if he continues to produce at the level he has in the last two seasons.
2025: 154 G, 130 OPS+, 45 HR, 110 RBI, 4.3 WAR
2026: 162 G, 144 OPS+, 42 HR, 101 RBI, 5.7 WAR
The Rays have never signed a player to a contract worth a guaranteed $200 million, but Caminero is a face-of-the-franchise caliber superstar worth committing a significant chunk of the payroll to for the foreseeable future.
The additional revenue that will come from their World Series trip, coupled with the potential for a salary floor to be instituted in the upcoming CBA negotiations, raises the chances of Caminero inking an extension.
The 11-year, $288.8 million extension Bobby Witt Jr. signed with the Royals is a reasonable starting point in negotiations, but we are inching closer to Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s 14-year, $500 million deal with every ball he sends into the seats.
SS Elly De La Cruz
4 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2029
The Reds have already approached Elly De La Cruz with an extension offer.
"We engaged in Spring Training of 2025 and presented an offer," Reds president of baseball operations Nick Krall told reporters in January. "The offer would have been the largest contract in Reds history. We didn't have any further conversations regarding the offer."
The current largest contract in club history is the 10-year, $225 million deal Joey Votto signed in 2012, so he has already had the opportunity to join the $200 million club and declined.
With Scott Boras as his agent and coming off the best season of his career, in which he showed improved defensive chops alongside his tantalizing power-speed combination, the likelihood of him signing an early extension is extremely low.
The Reds could eventually put him on the trade block if an extension doesn't work out. Any team acquiring him would likely want to get a long-term deal on the books. That provides multiple avenues for a huge payday in the coming years.
RHP Logan Gilbert
5 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2027
The volatility of pitchers makes mega contracts far less common, though Dylan Cease did reel in a seven-year, $210 million payday from the Blue Jays last offseason, even coming off an inconsistent contract year.
Over the last five seasons, Logan Gilbert has averaged 31 starts and 180.1 innings while posting a 3.46 ERA and 110 ERA+. That durability and consistency make him a prime candidate for a massive contract.
His 14.2 WAR over that five-year stretch ranks among the top 20 among all pitchers. Whether it's an extension from the Mariners or as the top arm in the 2027-28 free-agent class, a boatload of money is on the horizon.
The 29-year-old played on a $10.9 million salary last season. He is projected to earn $15.4 million in his final year of arbitration, which would make him an extremely attractive trade chip if Seattle decided to deal from its pitching depth.
SS Gunnar Henderson
6 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2028
In a down year by his own lofty standards, Gunnar Henderson was still a 3.2-WAR player, posting a 102 OPS+ with 57 extra-base hits and 24 home runs while starting 149 games at shortstop.
After a 6.1-WAR rookie season in 2023 and an 8.8-WAR follow-up season in which he finished fourth in AL MVP voting, he firmly established himself as one of the game's brightest young stars.
He looked like a clear long-term building block while the Orioles were on the rise, but their stalled progress toward contention led to the Adley Rutschman trade this past summer. That might not be the end of the roster turnover.
MLB insider Buster Olney made headlines in August when he said, "he's not going to sign there long term in all likelihood," while discussing Henderson's future. Whether he is the next homegrown star out the door or reaches free agency after the 2028 season, he will command big money.
1B Munetaka Murakami
7 of 10
Contract Status: One year, $17.5 million remaining on contract
Despite a prolific run in the Japanese League, Munetaka Murakami was not met with the robust market many expected last offseason due to swing-and-miss concerns. He signed a two-year, $34 million deal with the White Sox. That translated into him becoming the center of their surprising climb to the postseason.
The 26-year-old had a .207 batting average and 35.4 percent strikeout rate, but his on-base ability (16.6 BB%, .347 OBP) and power (130 OPS+, 35 HR) still made him one of the most impactful sluggers in baseball.
If he can match that performance in his second season stateside, a significantly more lucrative contract likely awaits in his next trip to free agency.
Pete Alonso got a $31 million AAV on a five-year deal ahead of his age-31 season as an elite power hitter with limited secondary value. Murakami will be four years younger when he shops for his next contract. Even if he doesn't match that AAV, a longer deal could easily push the full value above $200 million.
SS Jeremy Peña
8 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2027
At first glance, Jeremy Peña is not an obvious candidate for a $200 million deal, but never underestimate the earning power of a quality shortstop in a thin market at the position.
The 29-year-old has taken his offensive game to another level the past two seasons, logging a .291/.345/.477 line and 130 OPS+ despite missing some time to injuries. He remains a standout defender.
With 22.2 WAR over his first five seasons and a playoff track record few players his age can match, he would be an obvious extension candidate if not for the fact that he switched agents and hired Scott Boras in June 2025.
That clearly indicates he intends to test the market after the 2027 season, which could put him on the trade block this winter. Xander Bogaerts was the same age when he signed his 11-year, $280 million contract with the Padres. While he had a longer track record, Peña is a far superior defender.
LHP Tarik Skubal
9 of 10
Contract Status: Free agent
Tarik Skubal was the only 2026-27 free agent projected to earn a contract north of $200 million in my recent article predicting the 10 biggest contracts handed out in free agency this winter.
The nine-year, $324 million contract that Gerrit Cole signed prior to the 2020 season is a logical starting point, but Skubal could be aiming for a $40 million AAV given his track record and the rising cost of frontline pitching.
Barring a surprise mega-deal for Japanese League star Teruaki Sato, the odds are extremely high that Skubal will be the next free agent to lock in at least $200 million.
With a 2.42 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 655 strikeouts in 546 innings over the last three seasons, he has firmly established himself as one of the best pitchers in the sport in the prime of his career.
OF James Wood
10 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2030
One of the key return pieces from the Juan Soto blockbuster trade with the Padres, James Wood has developed into one of the best young sluggers in baseball and the face of the franchise for the Nationals.
The towering 6'6" outfielder has put together consecutive 30-homer, 3-WAR seasons. This year, he quietly developed into a more complete hitter beneath the surface of his 144 OPS+ and 30 long balls.
The 24-year-old raised his walk rate (12.3 to 16.4 percent), lowered his strikeout rate (32.1 to 28.7 percent) and added 21 steals in 25 attempts without sacrificing any of his power production.
After signing Cade Cavalli to a four-year, $47 million extension in September, the Nationals could be looking to lock up more pieces this offseason. Wood is the top candidate for a franchise cornerstone-level deal.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 MLB Postseason is entering the Championship Series, but the time for fantasy baseball analysis never truly stops. Last Monday, we started our Rotoworld Staff and Friends Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft for the 2027 season. While many places do a “too early” mock draft, we’d argue that it’s not really too early to look ahead to next season. I’ve been posting a collection of “look back” articles reviewing the best picks of the 2026 season, the worst picks, and my key lessons, but all of these articles are linked together by the idea that immediately taking stock in the season, before the offseason hype starts to creep in, can be an incredibly valuable experience.
So we invited our staff and a few of our friends to put together a 15-round mock draft that we’ll complete over the next couple of weeks and continue to break down for you in chunks over on our site. Today you’ll get the first four rounds, and then I’ll be back to update the next four or five rounds by the end of the week and then do one more update at the end.
We hope you find it a useful tool, and we’ll see how much it changes over the next few weeks.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft
| Round 1 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 1 | RotoPat (Rotoworld) | Shohei Ohtani | UT/SP | LAD |
| 2 | George Bissell (Rotoworld) | Pete Crow-Armstrong | OF | CHC |
| 3 | Frank Stampfl (CBS Sports) | Bobby Witt Jr. | SS | KC |
| 4 | D.J. Short (Rotoworld) | Elly De La Cruz | SS | CIN |
| 5 | Scott Pianowski (Yahoo Sports) | Fernando Tatis Jr. | 2B/OF | SD |
| 6 | Rivers McCown (Rotoworld) | Junior Caminero | 3B | TB |
| 7 | Matthew Pouliot (Rotoworld) | Aaron Judge | OF | NYY |
| 8 | Dave Shovein (Rotoworld) | Juan Soto | OF | NYM |
| 9 | Frank Ammirante (RotoBaller) | Jackson Chourio | OF | MIL |
| 10 | James Schiano (Rotoworld) | James Wood | OF | WSH |
| 11 | Justin Mason (FanGraphs) | Yordan Alvarez | OF | HOU |
| 12 | Jorge Montanez (Rotoworld) | Ben Rice | 1B | NYY |
Perhaps the story here is that no starting pitchers went in the first 12 picks. One season after Tarik Skubal, Garrett Crochet, and Paul Skenes either got hurt or had down seasons, none of the drafters seemed willing to roll the dice on a starting pitcher with their first pick. Honestly, I can’t blame them. Early-round hitters, on average, continue to out-produce early-round pitchers at similar draft costs. The pitchers that do hit can make a huge difference for your team, but the risk is exponentially higher. A hitter taken here who fails to produce value, like Kyle Tucker this year, can still produce $10 of value, but a pitcher who goes in the first round and fails to produce value is almost always due to injury, and they can give you no value.
We did see Pat still choose Shohei Ohtani (dual position eligible here) as the top pick over Pete Crow-Armstrong. There are certainly some questions as to whether or not Ohtani’s body can hold up to a whole season as a starting pitcher and a DH, which will bring some uncertainty to his fantasy value. We also know he’s clearly not healthy right now, so we’ll need to see if any of these injuries require offseason surgery, but PCA has certainly worked his way into the conversation to be first overall.
A big surprise for some might be seeing Fernando Tatis Jr. this high. The Padres outfielder was one of the best hitters in baseball from June 1st on after a batting stance change allowed him to clear his hips more easily and unlock the pull-side power that we know he has. He also picked up 2B eligibility this season, which will be huge for him at a pretty barren position.
Jackson Chourio and James Wood have used breakout seasons to propel them into the first-round conversation, and you have to wonder if there is yet another level of development there, and Yordan Alvarez now has outfield eligibility in all formats, which makes him an even safer pick here. There look to be plenty of outfield options in the first round, including injured New York stars Juan Soto and Aaron Judge. Both of them being in the first round makes sense, but we may start to have to ask real questions about Judge’s durability. He’ll be 35 years old next season. He’s a giant human being, and the strain of playing the outfield every day at that size takes a real toll on your body. The fact that his two major injuries this season were both soft tissue or muscle injuries (and not a broken toe) should begin to raise some questions about whether or not we can count on 150+ games from Judge going forward.
His teammate, Ben Rice, used a 40-home run season to catapult him into the first round as well. That’s without catcher eligibility. Rice was the first 1B off the board in this draft, and I really find it hard to argue against that. Some guys in the next round have an argument, but Rice is a tremendous overall hitter. He has clear power. He plays in a great park for his approach, and there is no way the Yankees are going back to regularly sitting him against lefties. Even if Rice is more of a mid-30s home run hitter going forward than a true 40+ guy, his approach at the plate makes me feel good about his contact and batting average, and that puts him ahead of the guys who will follow him in round two.
| Round 2 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 13 | Jorge Montanez | CJ Abrams | SS/2B | WSH |
| 14 | Justin Mason | Jose Ramirez | 3B | CLE |
| 15 | James Schiano | Jacob Misiorowski | SP | MIL |
| 16 | Frank Ammirante | Tarik Skubal | SP | LAD |
| 17 | Dave Shovein | Ronald Acuña Jr. | OF | ATL |
| 18 | Matthew Pouliot | Nick Kurtz | 1B | OAK |
| 19 | Rivers McCown | Jordan Walker | OF | STL |
| 20 | Scott Pianowski | Kyle Schwarber | DH | PHI |
| 21 | D.J. Short | Pete Alonso | 1B | BAL |
| 22 | Frank Stampfl | Corbin Carroll | OF | ARI |
| 23 | George Bissell | Cam Schlittler | SP | NYY |
| 24 | Roto Pat | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | SP | LAD |
And now the pitchers start to come off the board. Not really a surprise with who the first three arms were off the board: Jacob Misiorowski, Tarik Skubal, and Cam Schlittler. I assume those will be the top three arms in pretty much all rankings heading into 2027. Pat did snag Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the fourth starter picked in this round, and while some may argue for Chris Sale or Cristopher Sanchez here, there’s a strong case that Yamamoto could be locked into the fourth spot. There is still some elevated risk with starting pitchers in the second round, but at least every one of these teams added an elite bat in the first round, and both George and Pat were able to take second elite bats at the start of the third round, so this risk feels more palatable.
CJ Abrams is another player, like Tatis Jr., who picked up second base eligibility in most formats. That’s huge for his fantasy value. So is hitting .261 with 33 home runs and 34 steals while driving in 106 runs. Abrams will be 26 years old next season, and while his future in Washington is a bit cloudy, he’s an elite offensive talent who is finally making good on that promise.
We had some former first-round picks fall into the second with Jose Ramirez, Ronald Acuña Jr., and Corbin Carroll all falling into the second round. The falls make sense too. Ramirez and Acuña Jr. now just have a bit more injury risk than some of the other players going in the first round. Ramirez still has great upside at a position that lacks talent, which may drive his price up, but he’ll be 34 years old, and he hit just 12 home runs and batted .235 this year after hamate surgery. Are you willing to bet that he gets back to 100% of his old self, or do we think it’s more likely that he’ll be 75-80% of the guy who almost went 40/40 in 2024? Acuña Jr. is a harder bet because he has now played under 108 games in three straight seasons and has played over 120 games once since 2019. It’s hard to bet on a full season of production, and with PCA, Chourio, and James Wood emerging, it makes sense to go with the younger/healthier players.
At the same position, the most interesting name in this round is probably Jordan Walker. He had a breakout season this year, hitting .269 with 29 home runs, 102 RBI, and 22 steals. He also just turned 24 years old, so there is plenty of growth still possible for him. He struggled through an injury at the end of the year, which hurt his September stats, but there will be no half measures with Walker in 2027. You have to either be all-in on the fact that 2026 was a real breakout for a former top prospect or just acknowledge that you won’t be getting him in your drafts.
Pete Alonso and Nick Kurtz are the two first basemen I alluded to earlier who land here in round 2. Kurtz played just 99 games this season due to injury but still hit 21 home runs while batting .256. We know the hitting environment in Sacramento is elite, so he should still be going in this range.
| Round 3 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 25 | Roto Pat | Sal Stewart | 1B | CIN |
| 26 | George Bissell | Konnor Griffin | SS | PIT |
| 27 | Frank Stampfl | Miguel Vargas | 3B | CHW |
| 28 | D.J. Short | Cristopher Sanchez | SP | PHI |
| 29 | Scott Pianowski | Paul Skenes | SP | PIT |
| 30 | Rivers McCown | Mason Miller | RP | SD |
| 31 | Matthew Pouliot | Julio Rodriguez | OF | SEA |
| 32 | Dave Shovein | Trea Turner | SS | PHI |
| 33 | Frank Ammirante | Gunnar Henderson | SS | BAL |
| 34 | James Schiano | Jackson Merrill | OF | SD |
| 35 | Justin Mason | Kevin McGonigle | SS/3B | DET |
| 36 | Jorge Montanez | Jesus Luzardo | SP | PHI |
We see three current-year rookies go in Round 3, announcing themselves as top-tier talents for years to come, and it’s hard to argue against it. Sal Stewart, Konnor Griffin, and Kevin McGonigle all showed that they can handle this level of competition, and we should expect more growth from these young players. The same goes for Miguel Vargas, who is not a rookie but broke out in 2026 in a way that suggests consistent value. He’s always had an elite plate approach, and now he added pull-side power to that equation. Vargas will be 27 years old and is in an ascending lineup, so he belongs in this range.
We saw the next group of starting pitchers go with Cristopher Sanchez, Paul Skenes, and Jesus Luzardo. Obviously, the name everybody will want to talk about is Skenes. It was a bad year for the Pirates ace, and while he claimed he wasn’t hurt, his velocity fell throughout the year, and he was not missing as many bats. There had been some previous concerns that his fastball wasn’t a huge whiff pitch to righties (10.7% swinging strike rate in 2025), but Skenes saw huge strides there this season. However, that was basically the only place he got better, and by elevating his four-seamer more for whiffs, he also started to allow more hard contact. It’s hard to see Skenes being this bad again, but we also can’t ignore how this season went.
Mason Miller went here as the first closer off the board, and three former first-round picks fell in Gunnar Henderson, Trea Turner, and Julio Rodriguez. I covered Gunnar and Trea in my article on what I learned from the 2026 fantasy baseball season, so you should read that, but essentially their 2025 price baked in a full return to peak value and ignored the warning signs from that season. We don’t appear to be doing that this year.
| Round 4 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 37 | Jorge Montanez | Drew Rasmussen | SP | TB |
| 38 | Justin Mason | Chris Sale | SP | ATL |
| 39 | James Schiano | Francisco Lindor | SS | NYM |
| 40 | Frank Ammirante | Kyle Tucker | OF | LAD |
| 41 | Dave Shovein | Brice Turang | 2B | MIL |
| 42 | Matthew Pouliot | Zach Neto | SS | LAA |
| 43 | Rivers McCown | Oneil Cruz | OF | PIT |
| 44 | Scott Pianowski | Matt Olson | 1B | ATL |
| 45 | D.J. Short | Carson Benge | OF | NYM |
| 46 | Frank Stampfl | Chase Burns | SP | CIN |
| 47 | George Bissell | Hunter Goodman | C | COL |
| 48 | Roto Pat | Nolan McLean | SP | NYM |
Now we answer the question of how far Kyle Tucker falls as Frank Ammirante takes him with the fourth pick in the fourth round, 40th overall. I covered Tucker more extensively in my article revisiting the top two rounds of 2025 drafts, but the miss on Tucker was essentially looking at pedigree (his seasons before his last two injured ones) and also the team context (a move to the Dodgers) and ignoring that he hadn’t had a fully productive year in a while. I’m not sure anybody expected that Tucker would see his barrel-rate collapse and that he would make uncharacteristically aggressive, out-of-character swing decisions, so perhaps we can expect a slight bounce back to his previously healthy form.
Four more starting pitchers go off the board here, and it’s an interesting group. Drew Rasmussen was brilliant this season, but it was also his first over 150 innings, and he’s had three elbow surgeries. Can you bank on his health as your ace? Kind of the same question for Chris Sale, who will be 38 next year and has basically alternated healthy years with injured years. After being hurt for basically all of 2021-23, he threw 178 innings in 2024, then 125 in 2025, and then 163 this year. What’s in store for 2027?
The final two arms were young pitchers in Chase Burns and Nolan McLean. The Burns pick makes sense given his elite strikeout upside and plus raw stuff, but McLean is harder to see here. Not that he’s a bad pitcher, but taking him as the 11th starting pitcher is assuming tons of growth. His 26% strikeout rate and 16.6% K-BB% don’t line up with some of the elite arms in this range, and his 10.5% swinging strike rate continues to suggest some concern with his ability to consistently miss bats. He’ll be 26 next year, and he’s clearly a talented arm, but taking him this high means he really HAS to take the next step, or he won’t return value.
Oneil Cruz’s bounce-back season pushed him up into the fourth round, and he’s joined by young outfielder Carson Benge, who hit .282 with 20 home runs and 22 steals in his rookie season. He didn’t get the fanfare of the other rookies who went higher in this draft, but Benge has a true five-category skill set and should be in an improved lineup next season.
We also saw our first catcher go off the board in Hunter Goodman. Keep in mind that this is a one-catcher format, which is why you’re not seeing a lot of catchers go early, but George wanted to lock up an elite bat at the position. With Ben Rice no longer catcher eligible, Goodman was the top fantasy catcher this season after hitting 41 home runs, driving in 88 runs, and hitting .245 in Coors Field. There’s little reason to believe he can’t do it again.
| Round 5 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 49 | Roto Pat | Rafael Devers | 1B | SF |
| 50 | George Bissell | Cade Smith | RP | CLE |
| 51 | Frank Stampfl | Zack Wheeler | SP | PHI |
| 52 | D.J. Short | Parker Messick | SP | CLE |
| 53 | Scott Pianowski | Randy Arozarena | OF | SEA |
| 54 | Rivers McCown | Dylan Cease | SP | TOR |
| 55 | Matthew Pouliot | Vladimir Guerrero Jr. | 1B | TOR |
| 56 | Dave Shovein | Logan Gilbert | SP | SEA |
| 57 | Frank Ammirante | Garrett Crochet | SP | BOS |
| 58 | James Schiano | Bryce Harper | 1B/OF | PHI |
| 59 | Justin Mason | Logan Henderson | SP | MIL |
| 60 | Jorge Montanez | Michael Harris II | OF | ATL |
A few big-name starting pitchers with major injuries go in this round. Zack Wheeler (SP12) missed half of this past season after having thoracic outlet surgery, Garrett Crochet (SP16) missed basically the whole season with a shoulder injury, Dylan Cease (SP14) ended the season on the injured list with a shoulder injury, and Logan Henderson (SP17) has missed time in each of the last two seasons with injuries. We’re now outside of the top 10 starting pitchers, so these guys don’t HAVE to be your ace, but this is still an early round draft pick for pitchers who have some overall health concerns. I understand the argument for their upside, and while I may not make the pick here, that’s just my personal drafting philosophy.
Parker Messick (SP13) and Logan Gilbert (SP15) also go in this round. Both of them feel a bit safer from a health standpoint, and there is still an argument that Gilbert has another level of production to hit. I have him as a top-10 starting pitcher, so I like him going as the 15th starter off the board.
We see Cade Smith go here as the second closer off the board, and Rafael Devers and Bryce Harper make sense in this range as veteran 1B who are likely past their peak but continue to produce overall solid numbers. Devers really turned things around after a slow start to the year and seems as consistent as ever.
We also see two outfielders coming off big seasons in Michael Harris II and Randy Arozarena. James Schiano and I actually discussed this exact either-or in a video we recorded after the Braves were eliminated from the postseason. I picked Harris II easily because I believe in the changes he’s made over the last year-and-a-half, and I’m not looking to pay for Arozarena’s career year.
Lastly, we need to address Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who finally goes off the board here in the fifth. We all know how Vlad Jr. struggled this year, but he’s now going as the sixth 1B, late in the fifth round, which is way more palatable for me. I know the power wasn’t there, but we have enough of a track record to feel confident that he is at least a 20-25 home run bat who can hit .280 in what should be a solid lineup. That’s still a solid fantasy asset; it’s just not a pick to make in the first three rounds of your draft. Also, getting corrective eye surgery can’t be bad either.
| Round 6 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 61 | Jorge Montanez | Jac Caglianone | OF | KC |
| 62 | Justin Mason | Jhoan Duran | RP | PHI |
| 63 | James Schiano | Jazz Chisholm Jr. | OF | NYY |
| 64 | Frank Ammirante | Cal Raleigh | C | SEA |
| 65 | Dave Shovein | Andres Munoz | RP | SEA |
| 66 | Matthew Pouliot | Bryan Woo | SP | SEA |
| 67 | Rivers McCown | Drake Baldwin | C | ATL |
| 68 | Scott Pianowski | Alex Bregman | 3B | CHC |
| 69 | D.J. Short | Gavin Williams | SP | CLE |
| 70 | Frank Stampfl | Shea Langeliers | C | OAK |
| 71 | George Bissell | Kade Anderson | SP | SEA |
| 72 | Roto Pat | Wyatt Langford | OF | TEX |
This is a super interesting round to me, and I can’t make much sense of it, haha. There seem to be no runs here or any real trend.
We do get more catchers off the board here with Cal Raleigh, Drake Baldwin, and Shea Langeliers. It feels a little early to be in a one-catcher format, but everybody has their own strategy. Baldwin feels like a great pick after his 2026 season, and while I do think Raleigh is going to bounce back after a down 2026 season, I’m not sure he’d be the gamble I take this early in the sixth round. Yes, you might be getting 30+ home runs from that spot, but the batting average will be a drain, and we have no idea if that lineup will be any good.
Jhoan Duran goes off the board as the third closer, and then Andres Munoz next was a bit of a surprise. He wasn’t really in a closer committee in Seattle this year; they just didn’t get a lot of saves. His SIERA and underlying metrics look a lot better than his ERA, so it does feel like he was just unlucky, but I’m not that convinced the Mariners will be that good next year, and Munoz has never delivered as a consistent top 5-8 closer.
Three risky hitters with plenty of upside also go in this round: Jac Caglianone, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Wyatt Langford. We don’t really know where Jazz will be next year, but it seems like it won’t be New York. That’s likely a big park downgrade for him. His batting average also regressed pretty drastically this season, which had been a concern for him in previous years. We know the speed will always be there, so he’ll need to land in a park where the power can come as well, but this feels like a fair spot for him. Caglianone is also a popular breakout pick because his batted ball data has been really strong. I like the idea of him taking a big step next season, but a top-60 pick does feel like you’re paying as if the breakthrough is a given. We all know the deal with Langford at this point too. A top-70 pick on him feels right if he can stay healthy, but can he ever stay healthy?
Bryan Woo at SP18 and Gavin Williams at SP19 feel like strong picks at this point. Both of them have immense strikeout upside and the ability to be top-10 starting pitchers. Woo had a bad stretch this season but seemed to right the ship at the end of the year, and Williams still seems to have one iffy inning every game where his command gets wonky. However, the big surprise here was Kade Anderson. I know he was an elite pitching prospect, but he doesn’t have elite MLB velocity or Stuff+, which means that he gets by with command and a deep enough pitch mix. I think he will be a solid starting pitcher, but I’m not sure I see the ceiling to take him as SP20, especially in what will be his rookie season.
| Round 7 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 73 | Roto Pat | Henry Bolte | OF | OAK |
| 74 | George Bissell | Riley Greene | OF | DET |
| 75 | Frank Stampfl | Andy Pages | OF | LAD |
| 76 | D.J. Short | William Contreras | C | MIL |
| 77 | Scott Pianowski | Ceddanne Rafaela | OF | BOS |
| 78 | Rivers McCown | Byron Buxton | OF | MIN |
| 79 | Matthew Pouliot | Ketel Marte | 2B | ARI |
| 80 | Dave Shovein | Max Fried | SP | NYY |
| 81 | Frank Ammirante | Manny Machado | 3B | SD |
| 82 | James Schiano | Payton Tolle | SP | BOS |
| 83 | Justin Mason | Seiya Suzuki | OF | CHC |
| 84 | Jorge Montanez | Josh Hader | RP | HOU |
Round 7 gave us quite the run on outfielders. After Wyatt Langford ended last round, Henry Bolte, Riley Greene, Andy Pages, Ceddanne Rafaela, Byron Buxton, and Seiya Suzuki all came off the board in the seventh round. Bolte is the name that probably stands out. The Athletics’ rookie hit .277/.359/.405 in 119 big league games with 11 home runs and 21 steals. In 65 games in the second half, Bolte hit .289/.370/.448 with eight of his home runs and a 9.2% barrel rate. Bolte has always had loud raw tools, but he has struggled to lift the ball consistently, which has limited his power output. We started to see that a little more from him in the second half and, if it carries over, he has the makings of a 20/30 hitter in a great ballpark. Pat taking him at 73 means Bolte kind of HAS to get close to that in order to return value, which makes the pick a bit of a risk but not one without some logic to it.
The Buxton and Suzuki picks have their own risk too, along with clear upside. Buxton, who was coming off his best season in years, was limited to just 93 games because of a hip injury that ultimately required surgery. He’ll be 33 years old next season, with just one season over 105 games played since 2017 and coming off major hip surgery. A bit on him inside the top 80 is a huge risk, but we also know Buxton can produce fantasy value in 80-100 games. Suzuki is less of an injury risk but more of a team context risk since we have no idea where he’ll be playing next year. Perhaps it could provide a boost to his home run potential. Maybe the team context will limit his counting stats. We won’t know that for a while.
Two more starting pitchers also go here in Max Fried (SP21) and Payton Tolle (SP22), and, spoiler alert, one of them looks like a huge steal. When my starting pitching rankings come out later this week, I will have Tolle in my top 10 starting pitchers. He’ll be slotted right ahead of a tier of aces who have a history of injury (Crochet, Sale, deGrom, Wheeler), so maybe you want to call Tolle a top 15 starter if you’d take all of those injury risks over him. Still, getting a potential top 15 starting pitcher with pick 82 is tremendous. In case you think top-15 is rich for Tolle, he finished as the SP25 this season, and that was while recording just nine wins in 26 starts. He had a 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 28.4% strikeout rate and will be just 24 years old next season. As his breaking balls continue to develop, his performance should only improve.
| Round 8 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 85 | Jorge Montanez | Zack Gelof | 2B/OF | OAK |
| 86 | Justin Mason | Chase DeLauter | OF | CLE |
| 87 | James Schiano | Aroldis Chapman | RP | BOS |
| 88 | Frank Ammirante | Hunter Brown | SP | HOU |
| 89 | Dave Shovein | Freddie Freeman | 1B | LAD |
| 90 | Matthew Pouliot | Louis Varland | RP | TOR |
| 91 | Rivers McCown | Mason Montgomery | RP | PIT |
| 92 | Scott Pianowski | Mookie Betts | SS | LAD |
| 93 | D.J. Short | Tyler Soderstrom | 1B/OF | OAK |
| 94 | Frank Stampfl | Bryan Baker | RP | TB |
| 95 | George Bissell | Grant Taylor | RP | CHW |
| 96 | Roto Pat | JJ Wetherholt | SS | STL |
After Josh Hader went off the board in the last round as RP5, we got a run on closers here in the eighth round with Aroldis Chapman (RP6), Louis Varland (RP7), Mason Montgomery (RP8), Bryan Baker (RP9), and Grant Taylor (RP10). Hader and Chapman are the two established names among the group and make clear sense here, and Baker tied for the MLB lead in saves this season and will return for the potential World Series champion Rays. I’d say that makes him a solid top-ten closer. The other three are all bets on upside, and all bets that make sense. Varland was electric as a closer for the Blue Jays this season and finished as RP3 on the year. Taylor and Montgomery weren’t even full-time closers, and they finished as RP6 and RP7, respectively, due to their high innings totals and strikeout rates. The potential issue for both Taylor and Montgomery is that we have no idea if they will be used as traditional closers. Montgomery feels like the better bet since he had 18 saves this season, but it also took the Pirates a while to turn the role over to him, and they may prefer him in the “fireman” role in the same way the White Sox seem to prefer Taylor. That said, both of them are dominant relief arms.
Three young hitters also went in this round with Zack Gelof, Chase DeLauter, and JJ Wetherholt. Wetherholt as a top 100 pick after his rookie season makes sense, and DeLauter also clearly has the profile of a top 10 pick. His issue has been, and always will be, health risk. Yet, he did manage to play 133 games this season, hitting .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs and 11 steals. The hard-hit rates suggest that more power could be coming if he can lift the ball a bit more consistently.
Jorge’s pick of Gelof is also a bet that the 26-year-old really did reinvent himself this season, when he hit .256/.322/.475 with 22 home runs and 16 steals in 111 games. Gelof chased less outside of the zone, took a more patient approach overall, made more contact than he ever has, and was less pull-happy than he had been previously. All of that seems to suggest very real growth. Can the growth hold? That will be the big question you have to ask yourself if you draft him in the top 85 picks next season.
We also saw Hunter Brown go off the board here as SP23. If you had told people in March that you’d get Hunter Brown near the end of the eighth round, it would have seemed like a major coup. However, the Astros ace returned from a shoulder injury this season and never looked like himself. Is the injury still lingering, or was 2025 a bit of a fluke? Remember that he had a 3.49 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 25% strikeout rate in 2024. There was a major jump forward in 2025, but much of that was in the first half of the season. Even though his ratios remained strong after the All-Star break in 2025, his strikeout rate fell to 24%. So maybe Brown is more of a low 3.00-ERA pitcher who will post a 26% strikeout rate. That’s not a bad profile, but it’s not a top 15 arm. Then you have the health questions to factor in as well, so his slide here makes a bit of sense to me.

2 trades Astros must make this offseason after early postseason exit appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Houston Astros cannot react to an early postseason exit with minor roster adjustments. After finishing 81-81 and getting swept by the Chicago White Sox in the American League Wild Card Series, Houston needs to attack its two weaknesses: its rotation and an offense lacking speed and dependable outfield production.
This is still a roster built to compete around Yordan Alvarez, Jose Altuve, Carlos Correa, Jeremy Peña and Hunter Brown. However, the Astros need more than a depth starter and a platoon outfielder if they intend to make another serious run in 2027.
Houston should pursue two aggressive trades. Neither would be inexpensive, but both would address a major weakness without forcing the organization into a rebuild.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Trade for Mariners ace Logan Gilbert
Astros receive: RHP Logan Gilbert
Mariners receive: INF Xavier Neyens, RHP Ethan Pecko and OF Joseph Sullivan
Trading within the AL West would create an obvious obstacle, but Houston should still call Seattle about Gilbert. The 29-year-old is entering his final year before free agency, making him a logical trade candidate if the Mariners do not believe they can sign him to an extension.
Gilbert would give the Astros the durable frontline starter they lacked throughout 2026. He finished the season with a 12-11 record, 3.73 ERA, 1.09 WHIP and 205 strikeouts across 186 innings. His career numbers are equally strong: a 3.60 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 1,089 strikeouts over 1,021 1/3 innings.
Pairing Gilbert with Brown would give Houston two legitimate postseason starters and reduce pressure on a rotation ravaged by injuries. The Astros used a franchise-record 18 starters in 2026, and Brown lasted only two-thirds of an inning while allowing four runs in the decisive Wild Card loss.
Seattle would demand a premium for trading an established starter to a division rival. Neyens, Houston's No. 2 prospect, offers significant left-handed power, while Pecko supplies a near-major-league arm and Sullivan adds outfield depth.
That price would hurt a thin farm system, especially with Neyens ranked among MLB's Top 100 prospects. Still, prospects are assets, and Gilbert would address the Astros' most important weakness immediately. Houston should make the trade only with confidence that it can extend him beyond 2027.
Buy low on Jarren Duran
Astros receive: OF Jarren Duran
Red Sox receive: OF Logan Hughes and RHP Bryce Mayer
Duran's value dropped sharply during a disappointing 2026 season, creating a potential buy-low opportunity. He hit .207 with a .266 on-base percentage and .361 slugging percentage, although he still produced 20 home runs and 21 stolen bases in 151 games.
Those numbers are a significant step backward from his 2024 breakout, when he batted .285 with an .834 OPS, 21 homers and 34 steals. His combination of speed, extra-base ability and experience in left and center field would give Houston an element missing from its current lineup.
The risk is obvious. Duran struck out 165 times in 2026 and posted a .627 OPS, so Houston would be betting that a change of scenery and different hitting instruction could revive him. However, he remains under club control for two more seasons, giving the Astros time to recover value.
Boston would receive Houston's No. 3 prospect in Hughes and a pitching prospect in Mayer. Houston would keep its top prospect, Kevin Alvarez, while acquiring an athletic outfielder who could lead off, create pressure on the bases and move around defensively.
Neither trade guarantees another championship, but standing still is the greater danger. Gilbert would stabilize October pitching, while Duran would make the lineup faster and less dependent on home runs. Those are precisely the bold changes Houston needs after another brief postseason appearance.

Mariners’ Cal Raleigh, Josh Naylor undergo offseason surgery
Both are expected to be ready for spring training in 2027.
(Nick Cammett/Getty Images)
The assumptions were there during the season, the questions asked after. Monday morning came the answers as the Seattle Mariners announced the two players who struggled the most at the plate in ’26 had undergone surgeries, both performed at the University of Washington Medical Center on Oct. 3.
Cal Raliegh underwent a left shoulder acromioclavicular debridement procedure performed by Dr. Albert Gee. He is expected to be fully recovered prior to the start of spring training.
Josh Naylor required triangular fibrocartilage complex repair surgery on his right wrist which was performed by Dr. Jerry Huang. He is also expected to be fully recovered prior to the start of spring training.
For Raleigh, who also dealt with a right oblique strain that required time on the injured list, the procedure he underwent last week was essentially a shoulder cleanup. While it was clear the oblique played a part in his first-half struggles, Raleigh finished on a positive note, finishing just outside the top 40 in second half fWAR and 67th out of 164 qualified batters in OPS.
The story was different for Naylor, who was observed shaking out his right hand at the plate and wincing after some swings throughout much of the season. He too was dealing with wear and tear and it worsened as the season progressed, but he insisted on playing through.
“I think everyone plays through pain,” he told the media at his locker the final week of the season. “Everyone wants to play baseball, play at the highest level, and play at your best capability. Whether it’s 50% that day, give all your 50. Whether it’s 20, give your 20. But I don’t really like to use that as an excuse. If you’re not willing to play through pain, this is the wrong job.”
With his swing and the drop of his left hand there is little doubt there was a good amount of pain associated with playing through. The results, however, were not close to typical in terms of power with Naylor posting the eighth-worst slugging (.350) among qualified hitters and hitting just 10 home runs, which included just two coming after June 12. General manager Justin Hollander, during an appearance on Seattle Sports’ Brock and Salk, pointed to a different contribution Naylor made, however.
“Obviously, I think he dealt with some physical maladies that made it tough for him to get into his power,” he said. “I will give him credit. He found a way to get hits from May 1st on. He was one of the leaders in a hit for average in the league. He found a way to contribute to the team in a positive way, in a very Luis Arráez kind of way with a lot of hits and a lot of stolen bases and trying to do the best he could.”

item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Mariners seem likely to lose Randy Arozarena to free agency this offseason.
Those aren’t easy shoes to fill.
Arozarena has been a firm presence in the heart of the Mariners’ order for the past couple seasons. He also brings an energy and confidence that fires up the fans in the Pacific Northwest.
There really isn’t another guy quite like Arozarena out there, but if the Mariners are losing him, they have to at least consider what a replacement for him might look like.
The answer might not be out there in free agency. Instead, it might depend on Seattle’s pitching surplus to improve their roster on the hitting side of things.
Candidate to Replace Randy Arozarena
One candidate was suggested in a new article on Monday by Bleacher Report’s Kerry Miller.
The player: Emmanuel Rodriguez.
Rodriguez is a young outfielder who just made his debut for the Minnesota Twins this year.
“The Twins wouldn’t want to part with either Walker Jenkins or Kaelen Culpepper, but three guys a bit lower on their prospects list could be doable—with Emmanuel Rodriguez immediately becoming a candidate to fill the Randy Arozarena-sized hole in Seattle’s outfield,” Miller writes.
This is all in the context of Miller suggesting what he calls a “realistic” offseason trade for Mariners right-handed pitcher Logan Gilbert.
The package coming to Seattle would also including pitching prospect Riley Quick and infield prospect Ben Ross.
Rodriguez would be the centerpiece, though.
Rodriguez is 23 years old and originally from the Dominican Republic.
He’s been a top-100 prospect for each of the past four years in the rankings by Baseball America, MLB Pipeline and Baseball Prospectus.
Finally, he got to the bigs with the Twins at the end of the 2026 season. He went 8-for-45 (.178) with two doubles, a triple and two home runs. He actually had a 0.7 Wins Above Replacement in just 13 games thanks to a solid early impression with his defense.
The Mariners would have Rodriguez for the next half-decade if they made this deal, so it’d be worth considering.
Giving up Gilbert would be the tough part.
Case for Trading Logan Gilbert
If the Mariners were to trade Gilbert, it’d be because they have so much pitching depth.
He’s also entering the last year of his current contract.
“Between Emerson Hancock’s breakout, Kade Anderson’s arrival and Logan Gilbert’s projected salary of $16M in his final year of arbitration eligibility, the M’s might consider trading away the ace who was their Opening Day starter in both 2025 and 2026,” Miller writes. “At any rate, this starting rotation would still be quite formidable even without Gilbert. In addition to Hancock and Anderson, Seattle has George Kirby (through 2028), Bryan Woo (through 2029) and Bryce Miller (through 2029) for another two years. Ryan Sloan is also one of the top pitching prospects in all of baseball, and he might be a factor by the end of 2027.”
It’d be easiest to make this trade for Seattle if they can comprehend exactly what they’re getting in return. If they know they replace Arozarena’s spot in the lineup with an exciting young player, that certainly helps make the case for trading Gilbert.

Why Hyphen says Mariners need to ink Logan Gilbert to extension
Mariners analyst Ryan Rowland-Smith explains why keeping the right-hander is about more than just his performance.
(Olivia Vanni/Getty Images)
The Seattle Mariners have some heavy lifting to do this offseason as they attempt to bounce back from a disappointing 2026.
In addition to a managerial search, the Mariners have a few key players set to hit free agency, namely left fielder Randy Arozarena and longtime shortstop J.P. Crawford. And beyond those the soon-to-be free agents, they could also have an interesting decision to make with starting pitcher Logan Gilbert on the horizon.
Gilbert, who has a career 3.60 ERA and 1,089 strikeouts over 1,021 1/3 innings in six big-league seasons, will be in his final year of club control in 2027 and figures to be one of the biggest names to hit free agency after that season.
Seattle has yet to come to terms on any sort of contract extension with Gilbert, and reports of any extension talks between he and the M’s have been sparse.
So, with Gilbert entering his final year of club control with the possibility that he could leave afterwards, is he a trade candidate this offseason? Mariners analyst and former MLB pitcher Ryan Rowland-Smith doesn’t think that is a route the club should go with Gilbert. During Monday’s edition of Seattle Sports’ Wyman and Bob, Rowland-Smith explained why the M’s should lock down their talented right-hander with a new deal.
Rowland-Smith pointed to the way Gilbert pitched in what was a meaningless Game 162 for the M’s in their season finale as an example of why Gilbert needs to be retained.
“You got a dude who wants to pitch in (Game) 162, and the way he came out, it was not some wave to the fans and thank you. He (brought) the same intensity (he normally would),” Rowland-Smith said. “You need him when you’ve got a Kade Anderson, Ryan Sloan and so on to say, ‘This is how we do things.'”
In that final outing of the season, Gilbert struck out eight batters over four perfect innings before allowing a leadoff walk in the fifth that ended his day.
“Many guys would just say I don’t need to pitch… just have a bullpen day,” Rowland-Smith said. “Do you know how many guys I’ve played with who would do that? Do not get rid of Logan Gilbert – 1,000%.”
The 29-year-old Gilbert was one of just 13 pitchers to strike out 200 batters this season. He was also one of just five to do so while pitching at least 180 innings. The Stetson product has pitched at least 180 innings in four of his five full seasons in the majors, with the lone exception being in 2025 when he made the only trip to the injured list in his career.
“Pay the man. Have him here for a long time because he is so valuable,” Rowland-Smith said. “Logan Gilbert, sometimes I take him for granted. He’s, again, in the clubhouse and in that dugout, he is gold with some of these young players who you plan to bring up.”

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

28 Sep 2026, 10:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Ed Szczepanski)
Rookie Lucas Spence ripped a two-run triple to highlight a four-run third inning, helping the Houston Astros celebrate the American League West title with a 9-0 victory over the Athletics on Sunday in West Sacramento, Calif.
Christian Walker homered to lead off the sixth inning and joined Yainer Diaz, Cam Smith and Jeremy Pena in collecting two hits and an RBI for the Astros (81-81), who won the division for the eighth time in the last 10 seasons.
Third-seeded Houston will host the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Game 1 of the best-of-three wild-card series. The Astros went 5-2 against the White Sox this season.
Houston actually captured the AL West title prior to the conclusion of its victory, as the Texas Rangers dropped a 6-4 decision to the Minnesota Twins on Sunday.
Yordan Alvarez went 1-for-4 with an RBI single to boost his batting average to .316, giving him his first batting title.
Lawrence Butler had two of the five hits for the Athletics (64-98), who lost for the ninth time in 12 games.
Phillies 7, Tampa Bay 3
Zack Wheeler pitched six strong innings and Kyle Schwarber drove in two runs as the Phillies clinched their fifth straight postseason berth by beating the Rays.
Bryce Harper and Edmundo Sosa homered for Philadelphia, which had lost its previous four games by the combined score of 23-3. The Phillies finally showed signs of life in Game 162, and now they'll head to Atlanta to face the Braves in the National League wild-card round that begins on Tuesday,
Johnny DeLuca homered twice for Tampa Bay. The Rays earned a bye into the American League Division Series and face the winner of the wild-card series between the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox.
Cubs 6, Red Sox 2
Alex Bregman went 4-for-4 with two home runs and four RBIs against his former team to help Chicago wrap up the regular season by defeating Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The game was scheduled to be played in Boston, but was moved to Tropicana Field because of the nor'easter that hit much of New England throughout the weekend.
Both of Bregman's home runs came against Boston starter Tanner Houck, who made his first appearance on the mound since May 2025. Houck (0-1), who had Tommy John surgery last year, allowed three runs on four hits in three innings. The Red Sox were held to five hits and were 0-for-7 with runners in scoring position.
Twins 6, Rangers 4
Josh Bell hit a two-run home run and drove in three to lead host Minnesota to a season-ending win over Texas.
The loss eliminated the Rangers from the American League West title race and the playoffs. Rangers starter Mackenzie Gore allowed one hit and one run in 2 1/3 innings.
Twins starter Dean Kremer (5-5) gave up three hits and one run in seven innings. Kremer yielded a home run to Danny Jansen, but did not allow another Texas runner past first base.
Dodgers 5, Giants 1 (10 innings)
Andy Pages capped a four-run 10th inning with a three-run home run, and visiting Los Angeles beat San Francisco to earn its 100th win of the season.
The Dodgers took the lead in the 10th when Alex Call's two-out double off the left field fence drove in automatic runner Miguel Rojas. The Giants then elected to walk Max Muncy, before Pages foiled that strategy by driving a pitch by Duncan Davitt (0-1) into the left field bleachers for his 23rd home run of the season.
Alex Vesia (3-1), whose perfect ninth sent the game into the 10th, was credited with the win, which allows the Dodgers to take a three-game winning streak into their National League Division Series opener next Saturday against the winner of the wild-card series between the host Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies.
Marlins 5, Braves 3
Heriberto Hernandez and Griffin Conine slugged solo home runs, giving host Miami a win over Atlanta to end its season on a high note.
Marlins ace Sandy Alcantara tossed a scoreless ninth inning for his third career save. It was a fitting end of the year for Alcantara, who threw both the first and last pitch of the season for Miami. sStarter Janson Junk left with a no-decision. He allowed three hits and one run in 4 2/3 innings. Michael Petersen (4-4) earned the win with 1 1/3 hitless innings of relief.
Braves starter JR Ritchie (1-5) took the loss. He allowed seven hits and four runs in 5 2/3 innings. Mauricio Dubon hit his 12th homer to open the scoring and added an RBI single for Atlanta, which begins its home wild-card series against divisional rival Philadelphia on Tuesday.
Nationals 6, Mets 4
Andres Chaparro had three hits, including two solo home runs, and host Washington beat New York to end its season with a series win.
Will Dion (3-2) pitched two scoreless innings for the victory and Erik Tolman worked the ninth for his fifth save for Washington, which improved by 11 wins over 2025.
Francisco Lindor hit his 300th career homer and Ronny Mauricio smacked his third home run in two games for the Mets, who finished last in the National League East. Carson Benge ended his rookie season with three hits and an RBI.
Blue Jays 5, Reds 1
In potentially his final career start, Max Scherzer struck out seven over seven-plus innings and host Toronto topped Cincinnati.
The 42-year-old Scherzer (4-9) allowed one run and six hits to earn his 225th career win and boost his strikeout total to 3,557. The Blue Jays' 37-year-old designated hitter George Springer, who might have also played his last game, like Scherzer received a standing ovation when he was replaced.
Brandon Valenzuela hit a two-run home run for Toronto and Charles McAdoo added a solo shot in the rubber match of the three-game series. Brandon Williamson (5-5) allowed four runs and four hits in three innings for the Reds.
White Sox 4, Rockies 2
Randal Grichuk and Brenton Doyle smacked two-run home runs and Anthony Kay pitched five strong innings to boost host Chicago past Colorado.
The White Sox are set to visit the American League West champion Houston Astros on Tuesday in the opener of an AL wild-card series. Chicago clinched its first playoff berth on Thursday since 2021 but was eliminated from contention for an AL Central title with Saturday's loss to Colorado and a Cleveland victory at Kansas City.
Cole Carrigg homered for Colorado, which finished with more than 100 losses for the fourth successive season.
Royals 3, Guardians 2
Vinnie Pasquantino's second solo homer of the day broke an eighth-inning tie and sent host Kansas City to a win over Cleveland.
Jac Caglianone and Kyle Isbel each had two hits for the Royals, who ended a disappointing 2026 campaign by avoiding a sweep and winning for just the seventh time in the final 25 games.
Daniel Schneemann and Jo Adell each homered and had two hits apiece for the Guardians, who rested key regulars Steven Kwan, Jose Ramirez and Brayan Rocchio one day after securing their third consecutive American League Central title. Cleveland plays either the Chicago White Sox or Houston Astros in the American League Division Series.
Pirates 4, Tigers 2
Jared Jones pitched four innings of one-hit ball and Konnor Griffin led off the game with a solo home run and drove in two runs to lead Pittsburgh past host Detroit.
Griffin's homer was the sixth of his rookie season and helped the Pirates secure their first winning record since 2018 and only their second since last making the postseason in 2015. Jones was not eligible for the win after exiting the game before the fifth. Jones finished 5-6 with a 3.72 ERA in 21 starts after returning from elbow surgery in late May.
Rookie River Ryan (0-1) made his second start for the Tigers and sixth of his career. The right-hander allowed two runs on three hits over 1 1/3 innings. Detroit finished with a losing record after advancing to the American League Division Series each of the past two seasons.
Padres 9, Diamondbacks 4
Gavin Sheets homered and Freddy Fermin knocked in three runs as host San Diego tuned up for their National League wild-card series by stopping visiting Arizona.
San Diego, which opens its best-of-three series Tuesday night against the visiting Chicago Cubs, snapped a 4-4 tie with three runs in the bottom of the seventh. Fermin capped it with a two-run single.
Michael Soroka pitched 4 2/3 innings for Arizona, which was eliminated from postseason contention when Philadelphia beat Tampa Bay around the same time San Diego's Jake Cronenworth drew a bases-loaded walk to push home the go-ahead run in the seventh.
Brewers 6, Cardinals 4
Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his case for the National League Cy Young Award, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as host Milwaukee beat St. Louis to close with five consecutive wins and its franchise record for victories in a season (103).
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings and lowered his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. The right-hander struck out five, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Cardinals starter Andre Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings. He allowed six singles in the first inning for a 3-0 Brewers lead as well as Gary Sanchez's home run in the third.
Mariners 7, Angels 4
Logan Gilbert pitched four-plus hitless innings and struck out eight as host Seattle dealt Los Angeles its 100th loss of the season. It was also the last game for Dan Wilson as the Mariners' manager. The team announced after the game that Wilson will not return in that role in 2027 after a disappointing season and third-place finish in the American League West.
Jose Siri homered for the Angels, losers of 100 games for the first time. They had been the lone active MLB team to never suffer that many defeats.
Gilbert didn't allow a baserunner until walking Moises Ballesteros leading off the fifth. He struck out the side in the first inning to reach 200 strikeouts for the season, becoming the fourth pitcher in franchise history to do so in multiple seasons.
